query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing minor aluminum additions into equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, via arc melting, followed by standard solution treatment, will form a stable alumina-based protective oxide layer at high temperatures when exposed to air and maintain mechanical performance comparable to the unmodified alloy at both room and elevated temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy with 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C, as previously reported.
generation.intervention: Add a small fraction of aluminum (≤5 at.%) during arc melting, followed by standard solution treatment to promote formation of a stable alumina layer under high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
generation.conditions: Heat up to 800–1000 °C in air for 5–10 hours under representative loading conditions (strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1) to evaluate oxidation kinetics and mechanical property retention.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of an alumina-rich scale that serves as a barrier to oxygen ingress.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum segregates to the alloy–oxide interface and fosters the growth of a protective, thermodynamically stable Al2O3-based layer during oxidation, reducing internal oxidation and preventing embrittlement by slowing oxygen ingress.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Al-modified equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy will exhibit significantly reduced oxide scale formation and improved oxygen resistance at 800–1000 °C, retaining a higher fraction of its baseline mechanical performance than the untreated composition.
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr is susceptible to severe oxidation in air at high temperatures, with relatively high oxygen uptake and resulting mechanical degradation.
generation.boundary: Applicable within 800–1000 °C in standard atmospheric pressure for exposures of up to 10 hours under the tested strain rates (10−4–10−2 s−1). Performance outside these conditions remains unverified.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Al concentration for adequate oxidation resistance while preserving mechanical properties is not precisely established and requires further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr baseline samples and replicate samples with up to 5 at.% Al added, followed by identical solution treatments. Conduct isothermal oxidation tests in air at 800–1000 °C for 5–10 hours under tensile loading at 10−4–10−2 s−1 strain rates to measure weight changes and mechanical property degeneration.
measurements: Mass gain or oxide thickness over time
Oxide phase composition and scale morphology via XRD and SEM/EDS
Room- and high-temperature tensile properties and fractography to assess ductility retention
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If Al-added samples do not exhibit a lower mass gain, improved scale adherence, or retention of baseline mechanical properties relative to untreated HfNbTaTiZr, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Structural metallic materials for applications at high temperatures must have a balance of mechanical properties and oxidation resistance. Coated and internally cooled Ni-based superalloys are used in gas turbine engines close to their high temperature limit, which is imposed by the melting temperature of Ni. The search for new alloys with similar or better capabilities at higher temperatures has concentrated on Nb-silicide based alloys that have lower densities, significantly higher solidus temperatures in excess of 1900 °C and can offer notable mechanical properties []. For example, some of these alloys can have compressive yield strength of about 1800 MPa at room temperature, 1200 MPa at 1000 °C and 500 MPa at 1200 °C []. The oxidation resistance of Nb-silicide based alloys was improved dramatically when the key alloying elements Al, Cr, Si, and Ti were in synergy with other transition and refractory metals, for example Hf, Mo, and simple metal and metalloid elements, e.g., Sn [,,,,]. The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen to analyze the effect of each constituent elemental by the subtraction method and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were studied. Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. According to the experiment results, the effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on mechanical properties of equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys were described. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add an element which interacts frequently with the alloy, such as Mo. Oxidation resistance is one of the most important properties of high- and medium-entropy alloys and has been studied by many groups. Generally, the addition of Al, Si, and Cr elements in the alloy will significantly enhance the oxidation resistance of the alloy. For example, Sudeep et al. [] and Chen et al. [] proposed that the addition of Al and Cr elements helps AlCoCrFeNi2 and Al0.6CrFeCoNiSiX (X = 0, 0.3) high-entropy alloys to form a continuous oxide layer, which inhibits further oxidation. The addition of Si helps to promote the formation of a continuous oxide layer, which has a positive effect on the antioxidant behavior. The addition of V, Mo, and Ti elements will reduce the oxidation resistance of the substrate, which is not conducive to the improvement of the oxidation resistance of high-entropy alloys. For example, Cao et al. [] realized that Al addition resulted in better oxidation resistance by forming a protective oxide scale, but Mo addition weakened its protective effect. Lu et al. chosen.technique: arc melting followed by standard heat treatment and oxidation testing
chosen.conditions: assess oxidation resistance in air at 800–1000 °C for up to 5–10 h under relevant loading
chosen.why: Al additions can generate a stable protective alumina scale, thereby reducing oxygen ingress and preserving the alloy’s mechanical strength at high temperatures. This strategy directly addresses the identified performance limitation—the inadequate oxygen resistance—by targeting the mechanism of oxide-scale formation. The hypothesis is validated if Al-containing HfNbTaTiZr shows reduced weight gain and stable mechanical properties after high-temperature oxidation, and falsified if oxygen uptake and property degradation remain comparable to the untreated alloy.
